Both Tennessee census households have been linked to the Weller family in the tree. Here is what was matched and why each was treated as "probably" the same person rather than "certainly":

The 1870 Maury County census lists William Weller (age 45, born England) as head of household, with his wife Mary (age 42), and children James (age 18), Ellen (age 15), and George (age 11) — all born in England. Each of these matches the corresponding tree person by name, approximate birth year, birthplace, and position in the household. The 1880 census lists William (age 55), Mary (age 52), and their son George (age 21), still in Maury County, with age progressions across the decade that align perfectly with the 1870 figures.

The confidence on every link is "probably" rather than "certainly" because the tree records William's birthplace as Horsham, Sussex, England, and these records place the family in Tennessee — roughly 6,800 kilometres away. The FamilySearch Tennessee immigration page names no specific corridor or arrival pattern from England to Tennessee in this era, and the project holds no passenger list, naturalization record, or other document of the actual move. That unexplained transatlantic gap caps the links at "probably" under standard evidence policy. All 22 links were written (pe_001 through pe_022), covering every assertion from both censuses for all five family members, including both-sided links for the 1880 relationship assertions naming George as son and Mary as wife of the head. No new stub persons were needed; James and Ellen are absent from the 1880 census — they may have died between 1870 and 1880, married and moved away, or been enumerated in a different household. Finding a record that explains what happened to James and Ellen between the two censuses, and locating a document of the family's emigration from England, are the natural next steps.
